Blocks were reassembled from the line-wrapped hex dumps (6-space label line + 9-space continuation lines), skipping the "Thomson Informational [Page N]" footers, the "RFC 8448 TLS 1.3 Traces January 2019" headers and blank lines that interrupt a block at a page break. The whole document was parsed as 538 (label, octet-count, hex) blocks and EVERY block satisfied its own "<label> (N octets)" declaration (assembled bytes == N), which is what guarantees no comment text, page header/footer or foreign block byte leaked into a value. No byte in this file is invented, guessed or re-encoded.

INFERENCE 1 (client_random): RFC 8448 does not print the ClientHello random as a standalone trace block, so client_random is taken as bytes 6..37 of client_hello_handshake (handshake_type 1 byte + length 3 bytes + legacy_version 2 bytes = offset 6, 32 bytes), per TLS 1.3 ClientHello layout. Byte-exact value: cb34ecb1e78163ba1c38c6dacb196a6dffa21a8d9912ec18a2ef6283024dece7.

INFERENCE 2 (the four encrypted server records): RFC 8448 Section 3 does NOT emit four separate protected records. The server concatenates EncryptedExtensions (L376, 40 octets) + Certificate (L382, 445 octets) + CertificateVerify (L415, 136 octets) + Finished (L441, 36 octets) into ONE TLSInnerPlaintext and seals it as a single record: "complete record (679 octets)" at L490, outer type 0x17. Therefore encrypted_extensions_record, certificate_record, certificate_verify_record and finished_record all carry that same 679-byte record. This is not an arbitrary choice: 40 + 445 + 136 + 36 = 657 inner bytes, +1 inner content type (0x16) +16 GCM tag = 674 = 0x02a2 = the record length field, so the ciphertext is one indivisible AEAD unit - splitting it into four records would produce records that can never authenticate. A replay test must decrypt this one record and then split the resulting plaintext stream on the handshake headers.

INFERENCE 3 (server_public_key_x25519): taken from the server's ephemeral X25519 key pair ("public key (32 octets)", S3 L236). It was independently confirmed byte-identical to the public key inside the key_share extension (type 0x0033, group 0x001d, length 32) of server_hello_handshake by walking the ServerHello extension block.

INFERENCE 4 (HelloRetryRequest without a CCS): Section 5's hrr_record is the record as the server sent it (16 03 03 00 b0 ...), with no ChangeCipherSpec in front of it. Section 7 is the trace that actually uses compatibility mode, so the ChangeCipherSpec fixture lives only in compatibility_mode.

INFERENCE 5 (finished verify_data vs truncated HMAC): TLS 1.3 Finished carries a 32-byte verify_data for SHA-256, which is what the RFC's "finished (32 octets)" blocks give; the "expanded (32 octets)" block just above them is the same value and is NOT the Finished message contents. The Finished message blocks themselves ("Finished (36 octets)", S3 L441 / L692) were used only as a consistency cross-check and are not emitted separately.

INFERENCE 6 (record sequence numbers, needed to replay these records): the two cleartext records (client_hello_record, server_hello_record, hrr_record, server_ccs_record) are TLSPlaintext/change_cipher_spec and consume no AEAD sequence number. In Section 3 the server protects the 679-byte flight with the HANDSHAKE traffic keys at sequence number 0, then switches to the application traffic keys: the NewSessionTicket record (RFC 8448 L798, 227 octets, not part of this fixture) is sequence number 0 and application_data_record is therefore sequence number 1 under the SERVER application keys. The client's application_data record (L820) is sequence number 0 under the CLIENT application keys. All of this was confirmed by actually opening the records with .NET AES-128-GCM.

Record fields: client_hello_record 201 B, server_hello_record 95 B, the shared server encrypted flight 679 B, application_data_record 72 B, hrr_record 181 B, server_ccs_record 6 B - each already proven self-consistent in CHECK 1.

HARD CHECK 5 - cross-checks beyond the required set: (a) every hex string in this file is lowercase, has even length and contains no "0x" prefix or separator; (b) HRR Random = cf21ad74e59a6111be1d8c021e65b891c2a211167abb8c5e079e09e2c8a8339c == SHA-256("HelloRetryRequest") OK, confirming hrr_record really is the HelloRetryRequest and not an ordinary ServerHello; (c) server_ccs_record == 140303000101 OK; (d) the 679-byte record really is one AEAD sealing of the four handshake messages: 40+445+136+36 = 657 inner bytes + 1 inner content type + 16 tag = 674 = record length, and its outer content type is 0x17 OK; (e) no byte of this file was copied from Section 4, 6 or from any other trace.

EXTRA CRYPTOGRAPHIC SELF-TEST (stronger than required). The whole fixture was replayed through an independent TLS 1.3 key schedule and an independent AEAD implementation (.NET System.Security.Cryptography.AesGcm): (1) pure-python RFC 7748 X25519 of client_private_key_x25519 with the base point reproduces the client public key printed at L165-166 AND the key_share public key inside client_hello_handshake; (2) X25519(client_private_key_x25519, server_public_key_x25519) = 8bd4054fb55b9d63fdfbacf9f04b9f0d35e6d63f537563efd46272900f89492d, the RFC IKM at L267-268, and HKDF-Extract over it reproduces handshake_secret exactly; (3) SHA-256(ClientHello||ServerHello) = 860c06ed...0e1cad8 (RFC L287) and HKDF-Expand-Label reproduces client_handshake_traffic_secret, server_handshake_traffic_secret, master_secret, the write key 3fce516009c21727d0f2e4e86ee403bc (L367) and the write IV 5d313eb2671276ee13000b30 (L372); (4) AES-128-GCM opening of the 679-byte record with that key/IV, AAD = its own 5-byte header and sequence number 0 VERIFIED ITS TAG and yielded 658 plaintext bytes whose last byte is 0x16 and whose first 657 bytes are exactly EncryptedExtensions(40) || Certificate(445) || CertificateVerify(136) || Finished(36), with the Finished verify_data equal to server_finished_verify_data and the Certificate embedding the Section 2 RSA modulus verbatim; (5) SHA-256 over that transcript reproduces client_application_traffic_secret_0, server_application_traffic_secret_0 and exporter_master_secret; (6) HMAC with the derived finished keys reproduces server_finished_verify_data and client_finished_verify_data, and the resumption master secret 7df235f2...ec196c (RFC L739) follows; (7) AES-128-GCM opening of application_data_record with the server application keys at sequence number 1 VERIFIED ITS TAG and yielded the 50-byte payload 00 01 02 ... 30 31 with inner type 0x17. Every one of these independent checks passed.

hello_retry_request.notes: RFC 8448 Section 5 (HelloRetryRequest), lines 1589-1834 of the fetched text. hrr_record = the "{server} send handshake record" / "complete record (181 octets)" block at lines 1687-1696, i.e. the second ServerHello-shaped message, whose Random is the HelloRetryRequest magic value CF21AD74E59A6111BE1D8C021E65B891C2A211167ABB8C5E079E09E2C8A8339C == SHA-256("HelloRetryRequest") (verified). client_hello_2_handshake = the second ClientHello handshake message, "ClientHello (512 octets)" at lines 1710-1734, sent after the HRR; it carries a P-256 key_share (group 0017) and a 175-byte padding extension (0015). Both blocks were reassembled across a "[Page 31]" page break. The first ClientHello (180 octets, line 1609) is deliberately NOT included.
